content:
Advaita Vedanta and its central claim that Atman and Brahman are not separate.

What is Advaita?

Advaita means non-duality: the deepest self and the ultimate reality are not two separate things.

It is a school within Vedanta. Its best-known classical teacher is Shankara, who lived around the eighth century.

Advaita calls the deepest self Atman and the ultimate reality Brahman. Its central claim is that Atman is Brahman.

This is expressed in the statement Tat tvam asi: “You are That.”

What does non-duality mean?

In ordinary life I experience myself as one thing and the world as another. There is “me” here and everything else out there.

Advaita asks whether this separation is final.

Think of many pots filled with space. The pots have different shapes and names, but the space inside them was never truly separate from the space outside. The pot creates a boundary in our view, not in space itself.

Advaita says that our individual identities work in a similar way. At the everyday level we are different people. At the deepest level, consciousness is not divided in the way it appears.

Is Brahman a personal god?

Not in the ordinary sense.

Brahman is not a supernatural person sitting outside the universe and managing it. It is the non-dual reality of all things.

Advaita is therefore not straightforward atheism. It accepts an ultimate reality. But that reality is not the personal creator god rejected by many atheists.

What are maya and avidya?

Maya is the appearance of plurality and separation. Avidya is ignorance: mistaking that appearance for the whole truth.

A rope seen in poor light may look like a snake. The fear is real, but it rests on a mistake. Better light does not destroy the snake; it shows that the snake was never there as imagined.

Advaita uses this kind of example to explain liberation. The problem is not that reality must be replaced. The mistake in our understanding must be seen clearly.

Where do karma and dharma fit?

Karma means action and its consequences. Our choices create habits, shape character and affect other lives. Many Hindu traditions also understand karma across rebirths.

Advaita says that liberating knowledge ends the deepest ignorance. But this does not make conduct unimportant. A confused and restless mind is not ready to see clearly. Dharma, self-restraint and honest action prepare the mind for knowledge.

Must everyone accept Advaita?

No.

Advaita is one school of thought, not a belief that must be imposed on everyone. A person may find truth in dualism, devotion, materialism, scepticism or another path.

Each person is on a journey and stands at a certain point along the way. A teaching that helps one person may not help another at that moment.

The freedom to examine and choose matters. I may explain why Advaita makes sense to me, but I should not force it upon you.

Why do context and symbols matter?

Advaita often teaches through pointers, paradoxes and analogies.

The rope mistaken for a snake, space inside a pot and waves upon an ocean are not scientific models. They are symbolic representations meant to turn attention towards a question that literal language may hide.

A sentence can become nonsense when removed from its context. Before accepting or rejecting a teaching, I should ask who said it, to whom, for what purpose and at what level of explanation.

The symbol is not the reality. It is a finger pointing towards something to be examined.

What must a true seeker let go?

Ego.

The ego wants to collect Advaita as another identity: “I understand the highest truth; others do not.” That attitude contradicts the inquiry.

There is less that I know and much more to know. Patience is therefore not weakness. It protects me from mistaking a quick interpretation for understanding.

A true seeker must be ready to say “I do not know”, test their assumptions and let a cherished conclusion go. The aim is truth, not victory.

Does science support Advaita?

Science and Advaita can speak to each other, but they are not the same method.

Science builds explanations from observation, mathematics, experiment and results that others can test. Advaita uses philosophical reasoning, disciplined inquiry and examination of experience to ask what the self and reality ultimately are.

Quantum physics makes the physical world stranger than everyday intuition suggests:

  • Superposition means a quantum state can contain several possible measurement outcomes.
  • Entanglement produces correlations between separated systems that cannot be explained by ordinary local hidden instructions.
  • Measurement connects a quantum description to a definite recorded result and remains conceptually difficult to interpret.

These findings challenge simple pictures of independent objects carrying fixed properties. In that limited sense, they can feel aligned with Advaita's pointers about apparent separateness and the limits of ordinary perception.

But quantum physics does not prove Advaita. Entanglement is a precise physical correlation, not evidence that all minds are one. Measurement does not require a human consciousness in the simple popular sense. Brahman and Atman are philosophical claims, not variables in a physics experiment.

The honest position is neither rejection nor forced agreement. Science may give new occasions for wonder. Advaita may give language for a different kind of inquiry. Each must retain its own standards.

What follows?

Advaita asks me to look beyond the surface division between self and world.

If the same reality is present in all life, harming another is not merely harming something outside me. Compassion follows naturally from a deeper understanding of unity.

The idea should lead towards humility, not ideological domination.
